content: 1. Once-daily dosing of antiretroviral therapy (ART), particularly with efavirenz (EFV), may enhance patient adherence to treatment regimens. 2. Switching to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) from abacavir (ABC) may reduce the risk of exacerbating anemia, especially in adolescents weighing more than 35 kg. 3. Fixed-dose combinations of ART can be utilized when EFV is part of the regimen, aligning pediatric treatment with adult regimens. 4. For children on nevirapine (NVP), there is no immediate need to change the regimen, but transitioning to EFV may be considered, particularly for those aged three years and older. 5. EFV-based regimens, when combined with ABC or TDF, may improve adherence due to the convenience of once-daily dosing. 6. Nationally adopted criteria for treatment failure should guide decisions on regimen changes. 7. Long-term efficacy and safety of TDF, ABC, and EFV, as well as their recommended combinations, require further investigation. 8. Additional data are needed to evaluate the bone, growth, and renal toxicity profiles of TDF in children and adolescents, particularly in the context of malnutrition and stunting. 9. Adverse central nervous system effects associated with EFV during adolescence warrant further study to ensure safe alignment with adult treatment regimens. 10. Toxicity surveillance systems implemented alongside ART at sentinel sites can provide valuable data on the frequency and clinical relevance of these toxicities. 11. Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the most common opportunistic infections in children with HIV, necessitating the selection of ART regimens compatible with TB therapy. 12. For children younger than three years initiating ART while on TB treatment, recommended regimens include two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus NVP (ensuring a dose of 200 mg/m²) or a triple NRTI regimen (zidovudine [AZT] + lamivudine [3TC] + ABC). 13. For children aged three years and older, recommended regimens include two NRTIs plus EFV or a triple NRTI regimen (AZT + 3TC + ABC). 14. Children on standard NNRTI-based regimens (two NRTIs + EFV or NVP) who initiate TB treatment should continue their current regimen if on EFV. If on NVP, substitution with EFV or a triple NRTI regimen (AZT + 3TC + ABC) should be considered. 15. Triple NRTI regimens are recommended only for the duration of TB treatment, after which an age-appropriate protease inhibitor (PI)or NNRTI-based regimen should be restarted when rifampicin-based therapy ends. 16. EFV-based regimens are not recommended for children under three years due to insufficient pharmacokinetic data to ensure therapeutic drug levels when co-administered with rifampicin. 17. Routine laboratory tests, including HIV serology, CD4 cell count, and TB screening, are essential for HIV diagnosis and monitoring. Additional tests, such as hepatitis B and C serology, cryptococcal antigen testing (if CD4 ≤ 100 cells/mm³), and screening for sexually transmitted infections, may be desirable. 18. Monitoring during ART includes regular CD4 cell counts (every 6–12 months), viral load testing (at six months after ART initiation and annually thereafter), and assessments for potential drug toxicities, such as renal function for TDF and liver function for NVP. 19. Viral load testing is the preferred method for diagnosing and confirming ART treatment failure, defined as a persistently detectable viral load exceeding 1,000 copies/mL after at least six months of ART, with adherence support provided between measurements. 20. If viral load testing is unavailable, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure, with targeted viral load testing to confirm virological failure where possible. 21. Routine viral load monitoring (every 6–12 months) is recommended to detect treatment failure early and accurately, avoiding unnecessary switching to second-line ART. 22. Targeted viral load monitoring is less costly but may delay switching to second-line ART, increasing the risk of disease progression, drug resistance, and HIV transmission. 23. The threshold for defining virological failure is set at 1,000 copies/mL, based on evidence that low-level viraemia (50–1,000 copies/mL) during effective treatment does not significantly increase the risk of treatment failure unless sustained. 24. Clinical and immunological criteria for treatment failure have low sensitivity and predictive value for identifying virological failure, particularly in individuals initiating ART at higher CD4 counts. 25. Immunological and clinical criteria may misclassify individuals with adequate virological suppression as having treatment failure, leading to unnecessary switches to second-line therapy. 26. Further research is needed to refine immunological criteria for detecting treatment failure in individuals initiating ART at higher CD4 counts. 27. Viral load monitoring is increasingly recognized as the gold standard for assessing ART response, providing early and accurate indications of treatment failure and reducing the accumulation of drug-resistance mutations. 28. While randomized controlled trials have not yet demonstrated survival benefits of viral load monitoring over CD4 and clinical monitoring, longer follow-up is required to assess its impact on survival, resistance profiles, and HIV transmission. 29. The limited use of viral load monitoring in resource-limited settings contributes to lower-than-expected rates of switching ART regimens, underscoring the need for expanded access to this diagnostic tool.
